sword_marker_records.content_osis: <div sID="gen17470" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="13" osisID="Jer.13" sID="Jer.13"/> <div eID="gen17470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17471" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17472" type="x-p"/> Still the prophet is attempting to awaken this secure and stubborn people to repentance, by the consideration of the judgments of God that were coming upon them. He is to tell them, I. By the sign of a girdle spoiled that their pride should be stained, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.1-Jer.13.11">ver. 1-11</reference>. II. By the sign of bottles filled with wine that their counsels should be blasted, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.12-Jer.13.14">ver. 12-14</reference>. III. In consideration hereof he is to call them to repent and humble themselves, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.15-Jer.13.21">ver. 15-21</reference>. IV. He is to convince them that it is for their obstinacy and incorrigibleness that the judgments of God are so prolonged and brought to extremity, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.22-Jer.13.27">ver. 22-27</reference>.

that they might be unto me for a people, and for a name, and for a praise, and for a glory: but they would not hear. <div eID="gen17473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17474" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A sign, the marring of a girdle, which the prophet had worn for some time, by hiding it in a hole of a rock near the river Euphrates. It was usual with the prophets to teach by signs, that a stupid unthinking people might be brought to consider, and believe, and be affected with what was thus set before them. 1. He was to wear a linen girdle for some time, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.1-Jer.13.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. Some think he wore it under his clothes, because it was linen, and it is said to <hi type="italic">cleave to his loins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.13.11">v. 11</reference>. It should rather seem to be worn upon his clothes, for it was worn for a name and a praise, and probably was a fine sash, such as officers wear and such as are commonly worn at this day in the eastern nations. He must <hi type="italic">not put it in water,</hi> but wear it as it was, that it might be the stronger, and less likely to rot: linen wastes almost as much with washing as with wearing. Being not wet, it was the more stiff and less apt to bend, yet he must make a shift to wear it. Probably it was very fine linen which will wear long without washing. The prophet, like John Baptist, was none of those that wore soft clothing, and therefore it would be the more strange to see him with a linen girdle on, who probably used to wear a leathern one. 2. After he had worn this linen girdle for some time, he must go, and <hi type="italic">hide it in a hole of a rock</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.4">v. 4</reference>) by the water's side, where, when the water was high, it would be wet, and when it fell would grow dry again, and by that means would soon rot, sooner than if it were always wet or always dry. 3. After many days, he must look for it, and he should find it quite spoiled, gone all to rags and good for nothing, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.7">v. 7</reference>. It has been of old a question among interpreters whether this was really done, so as to be seen and observed by the people, or only in a dream or vision, so as to go no further than the prophet's own mind. It seems hard to imagine that the prophet should be sent on two such long journeys as to the river Euphrates, each of which would take him up some week's time, when he could so ill be spared at home. For this reason most incline to think the journey, at least, was only in vision, like that of Ezekiel, from the captivity in Chaldea to Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.3">Ezek. viii. 3</reference>) and thence back to Chaldea (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.24">ch. xi. 24</reference>); and the explanation of this sign is given only to the prophet himself (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.8">v. 8</reference>), not to the people, the sign not being public. God takes notice of the degrees of men's pride, the pride of some and the great pride of others; and he will mar it, he will stain it. Pride will have a fall, for God resists the proud. He will either mar the pride that is in us (that is, mortify it by his grace, make us ashamed of it, and, like Hezekiah, humble us for the pride of our hearts, the great pride, and cure us of it, great as it is; and this marring of the pride will be making of the soul; happy for us if the humbling providences our hearts be humbled) or else he will mar the thing we are proud of. Parts, gifts, learning, power, external privileges, if we are proud of these, it is just with God to blast them; even the temple, when it became Jerusalem's pride, was marred and laid in ashes. It is the honour of God to took upon every one that is proud and abase him.
entries.reader_content_osis: <hi type="super">1</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto me, Go and get thee a linen girdle, and put it upon thy loins, and put it not in water. <hi type="super">2</hi> So I got a girdle according to the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and put <hi type="italic">it</hi> on my loins. <hi type="super">3</hi> And the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me the second time, saying, <hi type="super">4</hi> Take the girdle that thou hast got, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon thy loins, and arise, go to Euphrates, and hide it there in a hole of the rock. <hi type="super">5</hi> So I went, and hid it by Euphrates, as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded me. <hi type="super">6</hi> And it came to pass after many days, that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto me, Arise, go to Euphrates, and take the girdle from thence, which I commanded thee to hide there. <hi type="super">7</hi> Then I went to Euphrates, and digged, and took the girdle from the place where I had hid it: and, behold, the girdle was marred, it was profitable for nothing. <hi type="super">8</hi> Then the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">9</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , After this manner will I mar the pride of Judah, and the great pride of Jerusalem. <hi type="super">10</hi> This evil people, which refuse to hear my words, which walk in the imagination of their heart, and walk after other gods, to serve them, and to worship them, shall even be as this girdle, which is good for nothing. <hi type="super">11</hi> For as the girdle cleaveth to the loins of a man, so have I caused to cleave unto me the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; that they might be unto me for a people, and for a name, and for a praise, and for a glory: but they would not hear. <div eID="gen17473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17474" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A sign, the marring of a girdle, which the prophet had worn for some time, by hiding it in a hole of a rock near the river Euphrates. It was usual with the prophets to teach by signs, that a stupid unthinking people might be brought to consider, and believe, and be affected with what was thus set before them. 1. He was to wear a linen girdle for some time, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.1-Jer.13.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. Some think he wore it under his clothes, because it was linen, and it is said to <hi type="italic">cleave to his loins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.13.11">v. 11</reference>. It should rather seem to be worn upon his clothes, for it was worn for a name and a praise, and probably was a fine sash, such as officers wear and such as are commonly worn at this day in the eastern nations. He must <hi type="italic">not put it in water,</hi> but wear it as it was, that it might be the stronger, and less likely to rot: linen wastes almost as much with washing as with wearing. Being not wet, it was the more stiff and less apt to bend, yet he must make a shift to wear it. Probably it was very fine linen which will wear long without washing. The prophet, like John Baptist, was none of those that wore soft clothing, and therefore it would be the more strange to see him with a linen girdle on, who probably used to wear a leathern one. 2. After he had worn this linen girdle for some time, he must go, and <hi type="italic">hide it in a hole of a rock</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.4">v. 4</reference>) by the water's side, where, when the water was high, it would be wet, and when it fell would grow dry again, and by that means would soon rot, sooner than if it were always wet or always dry. 3. After many days, he must look for it, and he should find it quite spoiled, gone all to rags and good for nothing, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.7">v. 7</reference>. It has been of old a question among interpreters whether this was really done, so as to be seen and observed by the people, or only in a dream or vision, so as to go no further than the prophet's own mind. It seems hard to imagine that the prophet should be sent on two such long journeys as to the river Euphrates, each of which would take him up some week's time, when he could so ill be spared at home. For this reason most incline to think the journey, at least, was only in vision, like that of Ezekiel, from the captivity in Chaldea to Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.3">Ezek. viii. 3</reference>) and thence back to Chaldea (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.24">ch. xi. 24</reference>); and the explanation of this sign is given only to the prophet himself (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.8">v. 8</reference>), not to the people, the sign not being public. But there being, it is probable, at that time, great conveniences of travelling between Jerusalem and Babylon, and some part of Euphrates being not so far off but that it was made the utmost border of the land of promise (<reference osisRef="Josh.1.4">Josh. i. 4</reference>), I see no inconvenience in supposing the prophet to have made two journeys thither; for it is expressly said, <hi type="italic">He did as the Lord commanded him;</hi> and thus gave a signal proof of his obsequiousness to his God, to shame the stubbornness of a disobedient people: the toil of his journey would be very proper to signify both the pains they took to corrupt themselves with their idolatries and the sad fatigue of their captivity; and Euphrates being the river of Babylon, which was to be the place of their bondage, was a material circumstance in this sign. <div eID="gen17474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17475" type="x-p"/> II. The thing signified by this sign. The prophet was willing to be at any cost and pains to affect this people with the word of the Lord. Ministers must spend, and be spent, for the good of souls. We have the explanation of this sign, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.9-Jer.13.11">v. 9-11</reference>. <div eID="gen17475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17476" type="x-p"/> 1. The people of Israel had been to God as this girdle in two respects:—(1.) He had taken them into covenant and communion with himself: <hi type="italic">As the girdle cleaves</hi> very closely <hi type="italic">to the loins of a man</hi> and surrounds him, <hi type="italic">so have I caused to cleave to me the houses of Israel and Judah.</hi> They were a people near to God (<reference osisRef="Ps.148.14">Ps. cxlviii. 14</reference>); they were his own, a peculiar people to him, a kingdom of priests that had access to him above other nations. He <hi type="italic">caused them to cleave</hi> to him by the law he gave them, the prophets he sent among them, and the favours which in his providence he showed them. He required their stated attendance in the courts of his house, and the frequent ratification of their covenant with him by sacrifices. Thus they were made so as to cleave to him that one would think they could never have been parted. (2.) He had herein designed his own honour. When he took them to be <hi type="italic">to him for a people,</hi> it was that they might be to him <hi type="italic">for a name, and for a praise, and for a glory,</hi> as a girdle is an ornament to a man, and particularly the <hi type="italic">curious girdle of the ephod</hi> was to the high-priest <hi type="italic">for glory and for beauty.</hi> Note, Those whom God takes to be to him for a people he intends to be to him for a praise. [1.] It is their duty to honour him, by observing his institutions and aiming therein at his glory, and thus adorning their profession. [2.] It is their happiness that he reckons himself honoured in them and by them. He is pleased with them, and glories in his relation to them, while they behave themselves as become his people. He was pleased to take it among the titles of his honour to be <hi type="italic">the God of Israel,</hi> even a <hi type="italic">God to Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.17.24">1 Chron. xvii. 24</reference>. In vain do we pretend to be to God for a people if we be not to him for a praise. <div eID="gen17476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17477" type="x-p"/> 2. They had by their idolatries and other iniquities loosed themselves from him, thrown themselves at a distance, robbed him of the honour they owed him, buried themselves in the earth, and foreign earth too, mingled among the nations, and were so spoiled and corrupted that they were <hi type="italic">good for nothing:</hi> they could no more be to God, as they were designed, <hi type="italic">for a name and a praise,</hi> for they would not hear either their duty to do it or their privilege to value it: <hi type="italic">They refused to hear the words of God,</hi> by which they might have been kept still cleaving closely to him. <hi type="italic">They walked in the imagination of their heart,</hi> wherever their fancy led them; and denied themselves no gratification they had a mind to, particularly in their worship. They would not <hi type="italic">cleave to God,</hi> but <hi type="italic">walked after other gods, to serve them,</hi> and <hi type="italic">to worship them;</hi> they doted upon the gods of the heathen nations that lay towards Euphrates, so that they were quite spoiled for the service of their own God, and were as <hi type="italic">this girdle,</hi> this rotten girdle, a disgrace to their profession and not an ornament. A thousand pities it was that such a girdle should be so spoiled, that such a people should so wretchedly degenerate. <div eID="gen17477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17478" type="x-p"/> 3. God would by his judgments separate them from him, send them into captivity, deface all their beauty and ruin their excellency, so that they should be like a fine girdle gone to rags, a worthless, useless, despicable people. God will after this manner <hi type="italic">mar the pride of Judah, and the great pride of Jerusalem.</hi> He would strip them of all that which was the matter of their pride, of which they boasted and in which they trusted; it should not only be sullied and stained, but quite destroyed, like this linen girdle. Observe, He speaks of <hi type="italic">the pride of Judah</hi> (the country people were proud of their holy land, their good land), but of <hi type="italic">the great pride of Jerusalem;</hi> there the temple was, and the royal palace, and therefore those citizens were more proud than the inhabitants of other cities. God takes notice of the degrees of men's pride, the pride of some and the great pride of others; and he will mar it, he will stain it. Pride will have a fall, for God resists the proud. He will either mar the pride that is in us (that is, mortify it by his grace, make us ashamed of it, and, like Hezekiah, humble us for the pride of our hearts, the great pride, and cure us of it, great as it is; and this marring of the pride will be making of the soul; happy for us if the humbling providences our hearts be humbled) or else he will mar the thing we are proud of. Parts, gifts, learning, power, external privileges, if we are proud of these, it is just with God to blast them; even the temple, when it became Jerusalem's pride, was marred and laid in ashes. It is the honour of God to <hi type="italic">took upon every one that is proud and abase him.</hi>

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen17478" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Bottles Filled with Wine; Punishment Predicted; A Call to Repentance. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  606.)</title> <div sID="gen17479" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Therefore thou shalt speak unto them this word; Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, Every bottle shall be filled with wine: and they shall say unto thee, Do we not certainly know that every bottle shall be filled with wine? <hi type="super">13</hi> Then shalt thou say unto them, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Behold, I will fill all the inhabitants of this land, even the kings that sit upon David's throne, and the priests, and the prophets, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, with drunkenness. <hi type="super">14</hi> And I will dash them one against another, even the fathers and the sons together, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : I will not pity, nor spare, nor have mercy, but destroy them. <hi type="super">15</hi> Hear ye, and give ear; be not proud: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoken. <hi type="super">16</hi> Give glory to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, before he cause darkness, and before your feet stumble upon the dark mountains, and, while ye look for light, he turn it into the shadow of death, <hi type="italic">and</hi> make <hi type="italic">it</hi> gross darkness. <hi type="super">17</hi> But if ye will not hear it, my soul shall weep in secret places for <hi type="italic">your</hi> pride; and mine eye shall weep sore, and run down with tears, because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's flock is carried away captive. <hi type="super">18</hi> Say unto the king and to the queen, Humble yourselves, sit down: for your principalities shall come down, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the crown of your glory. <hi type="super">19</hi> The cities of the south shall be shut up, and none shall open <hi type="italic">them:</hi> Judah shall be carried away captive all of it, it shall be wholly carried away captive. <hi type="super">20</hi> Lift up your eyes, and behold them that come from the north: where <hi type="italic">is</hi> the flock <hi type="italic">that</hi> was given thee, thy beautiful flock? <hi type="super">21</hi> What wilt thou say when he shall punish thee? for thou hast taught them <hi type="italic">to be</hi> captains, <hi type="italic">and</hi> as chief over thee: shall not sorrows take thee, as a woman in travail? <div eID="gen17479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17480" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A judgment threatened against this people that would quite intoxicate them. This doom is pronounced against them in a figure, to make it the more taken notice of and the more affecting (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, every bottle shall be filled with wine;</hi> that is, those that by their sins have made themselves <hi type="italic">vessels of wrath fitted to destruction</hi> shall be filled with the wrath of God as a bottle is with wine; and, as every vessel of mercy prepared for glory shall be filled with mercy and glory, so they shall <hi type="italic">be full of the fury of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.20">Isa. li. 20</reference>); and they shall be brittle as bottles; and, like old bottles into which new wine is put, they shall burst and be broken to pieces, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.17">Matt. ix. 17</reference>. Or, They shall have their heads as full of wine as bottle are; for so it is explained, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.13">v. 13</reference>, <hi type="italic">They shall be filled with drunkenness;</hi> compare <reference osisRef="Isa.51.17">Isa. li. 17</reference>. It is probable that this was a common proverb among them, applied in various ways; but they, not being aware of the prophet's meaning in it, ridiculed him for it: "<hi type="italic">Do we not certainly know</hi> that <hi type="italic">every bottle shall be filled with wine?</hi> What strange thing is there in that? Tell us something that we did not know before." Perhaps they were thus touchy with the prophet because they apprehended this to be a reflection upon them for their drunkenness, and probably it was in part so intended. They <hi type="italic">loved flagons of wine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.3.1">Hos. iii. 1</reference>. Their watchmen were all <hi type="italic">for wine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.56.12">Isa. lvi. 12</reference>. They loved their false prophets <hi type="italic">that prophesied to them of wine</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.11">Mic. ii. 11</reference>), that bade them be merry, for that they should never want their bottle to make them so. "Well," says the prophet, "you shall have your <hi type="italic">bottles full of wine,</hi> but not such wine as you desire." They suspected that he had some mystical meaning in it which prophesied no good concerning them, but evil; and he owns that so he had. What he meant was this, <div eID="gen17480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17481" type="x-p"/> 1. That they should be a giddy as men in drink. A drunken man is fitly compared to a bottle or cask full of wine; for, when the wine is in, the wit, and wisdom, and virtue, and all that is good for any thing, are out. Now God threatens (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.13">v. 13</reference>) that shall they shall all be <hi type="italic">filled with drunkenness;</hi> they shall be full of confusion in their counsels, shall falter in all their talk and stagger in all their motions; they shall not know what they say or do, much less what they should say or do. They shall be sick of all their enjoyments and throw them up as drunken men do, <reference osisRef="Job.20.15">Job xx. 15</reference>. They shall fall into a slumber, and be utterly unable to help themselves, and, like men that have drunk away their reason, shall lie at the mercy and expose themselves to the contempt of all about them. And this shall be the condition not of some among them (if any had been sober, they might have helped the rest), but <hi type="italic">even the kings that sit upon the throne of David,</hi> that should have been like their father David, who was <hi type="italic">wise as an angel of God,</hi> shall be thus intoxicated. Their priests and prophets too, their false prophets, that pretended to guide them, were as indulgent of their lusts, and therefore were justly as much deprived of their senses, as any other. Nay, <hi type="italic">all the inhabitants,</hi> both <hi type="italic">of the land</hi> and <hi type="italic">of Jerusalem</hi> were as far gone as they. Whom God will destroy he infatuates. <div eID="gen17481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17482" type="x-p"/> 2. That, being giddy, they should run upon one another. The cup of the wine of the Lord's fury shall throw them not only into a lethargy, so that they shall not be able to help themselves or one another, but into a perfect frenzy, so that they shall do mischief to themselves and one another (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will dash a man against his brother.</hi> Not only their drunken follies, but their drunken frays, shall help to ruin them. Drunken men are often quarrelsome, and upon that account they have <hi type="italic">woe and sorrow</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.29-Prov.23.30">Prov. xxiii. 29, 30</reference>); so their sin is their punishment; it was so here. God sent an evil spirit into families and neighbourhoods (as <reference osisRef="Judg.9.23">Judg. ix. 23</reference>), which made them jealous of, and spiteful towards, one another; so that <hi type="italic">the fathers and sons</hi> went <hi type="italic">together</hi> by the ears, and were ready to pull one another to pieces, which made them all an easy prey to the common enemy. This decree against them having gone forth, God says, <hi type="italic">I will not pity, nor spare, nor have mercy, but destroy them;</hi> for they <hi type="italic">will not pity, nor spare, nor have mercy,</hi> but destroy one another; see <reference osisRef="Hab.2.15-Hab.2.16">Hab. ii. 15, 16</reference>. <div eID="gen17482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17483" type="x-p"/> II. Here is good counsel given, which, if taken, would prevent this desolation. It is, in short, to <hi type="italic">humble themselves under the mighty hand of God.</hi> If they will <hi type="italic">hearken and give ear,</hi> this is that which God has to say to them, <hi type="italic">Be not proud,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.13.15">v. 15</reference>. This was one of the sins for which God had a controversy with them (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.9">v. 9</reference>); let them mortify and forsake this sin, and God will let fall his controversy. "<hi type="italic">Be not proud.;</hi> when God speaks to you by his prophets do not think yourselves too good to be taught; be not scornful, be not wilful, let not your hearts rise against the word, nor slight the messengers that bring it to you. When God is coming forth against you in his providence (and by them he speaks) be not secure when he threatens, be not impatient when he strikes, for pride is at the bottom of both." It is the great God that has spoken, whose authority is incontestable, whose power is irresistible; therefore bow to what he says, and <hi type="italic">be not proud,</hi> as you have been. They must not be proud, for, <div eID="gen17483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17484" type="x-p"/> 1. They must advance God, and study how to do him honour: "Give <hi type="italic">glory to the Lord your God,</hi> and not to your idols, not to other gods. Give him glory by confessing your sins, owning yourselves guilty before him, and accepting the punishment of your iniquity, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.16">v. 16</reference>. Give him glory by a sincere repentance and reformation." Then and not till then, we begin to live as we should, and to some good purpose, when we begin to <hi type="italic">give glory to the Lord our God,</hi> to make his honour our chief end and to seek it accordingly. "Do this quickly, while your space to repent is continued to you; <hi type="italic">before he cause darkness,</hi> before you will see no way of escaping." Note, Darkness will be the portion of those that will not repent to <hi type="italic">give glory to God.</hi> When those that by the fourth vial were scorched with heat <hi type="italic">repented not, to give glory to God,</hi> the next vial filled them with <hi type="italic">darkness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.16.9-Rev.16.10">Rev. xvi. 9, 10</reference>. The aggravation of the darkness here threatened is, (1.) That their attempts to escape shall hasten their ruin: <hi type="italic">Their feet shall stumble</hi> when they are making all the haste they can over <hi type="italic">the dark mountains,</hi> and they shall fall, and be unable to get up again. Note, Those that think to out-run the judgments of God will find their road impassable; let them make the best of their way, they can make nothing of it, the judgments that pursue them will overtake them; their way is dark and slippery, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.6">Ps. xxxv. 6</reference>. And therefore, before it comes to that extremity, it is our wisdom to give glory to him, and so make our peace with him, to fly to his mercy, and then there will be no occasion to fly from his justice. (2.) That their hopes of a better state of things will be disappointed: <hi type="italic">While you look for light,</hi> for comfort and relief, he will <hi type="italic">turn it into the shadow of death,</hi> which is very dismal and terrible, and make it <hi type="italic">gross darkness,</hi> like that of Egypt, when Pharaoh continued to harden his heart, which was darkness that might be felt. The expectation of impenitent sinners perishes when they die and think to have it satisfied. <div eID="gen17484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17485" type="x-p"/> 2. They must abase themselves, and take shame to themselves; the prerogative of the king and queen will not exempt them from this (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Say to the king and queen,</hi> that, great as they are, they must <hi type="italic">humble themselves</hi> by true repentance, and so give both glory to God and a good example to their subjects." Note, Those that are exalted above others in the world must humble themselves before God, who is higher than the highest, and to whom kings and queens are accountable. They must <hi type="italic">humble themselves,</hi> and <hi type="italic">sit down</hi>—sit down, and consider what is coming—sit down in the dust, and lament themselves. Let them humble themselves, for God will otherwise take an effectual course to humble them: "<hi type="italic">Your principalities shall come down,</hi> the honour and power on which you value yourselves and in which you confide, <hi type="italic">even the crown of your glory,</hi> your <hi type="italic">goodly or glorious crown:</hi> when you are led away captives, where will your principality and all the badges of it be then?" Blessed be God there is a crown of glory, which those shall inherit who do humble themselves, that shall never <hi type="italic">come down.</hi> <div eID="gen17485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17486" type="x-p"/> III. This counsel is enforced by some arguments if they continue proud and unhumbled. <div eID="gen17486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17487" type="x-p"/> 1. It will be the prophet's unspeakable grief (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.17">v. 17</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If you will not hear it,</hi> will not submit to the word, but continue refractory, not only my eye, but <hi type="italic">my soul shall weep in secret places.</hi>" Note, The obstinacy of people, in refusing to hear the word of God, will be heart-breaking to the poor ministers, who know something of the terrors of the Lord and the worth of souls, and are so far from desiring that they tremble at the thoughts of the death of sinners. His grief for it was undissembled (his <hi type="italic">soul wept</hi>) and void of affectation, for he chose to weep <hi type="italic">in secret places,</hi> where no eye saw him but his who is all eye. He would mingle his tears not only with his public preaching, but with his private devotions. Nay, thoughts of their case would make him melancholy, and he would become a perfect recluse. It would grieve him, (1.) To see their sins unrepented of: "<hi type="italic">My soul shall weep for your pride,</hi> your haughtiness, and stubbornness, and vain confidence." Note, The sins of others should be matter of sorrow to us. We must mourn for that which we cannot mend, and mourn the more for it because we cannot mend it. (2.) To see their calamity past redress and remedy: "<hi type="italic">My eyes shall weep sorely,</hi> not so much because my relations, friends, and neighbours are in distress, but <hi type="italic">because the Lord's flock,</hi> his people and the sheep of his pasture, <hi type="italic">are carried away captive.</hi>" That should always grieve us most by which God's honour suffers and the interest of his kingdom is weakened. <div eID="gen17487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17488" type="x-p"/> 2. It will be their own inevitable ruin, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.19-Jer.13.21">v. 19-21</reference>. (1.) The land shall be laid waste: <hi type="italic">The cities of the south shall be shut up.</hi> The cities of Judah lay in the southern part of the land of Canaan; these shall be straitly besieged by the enemy, so that there shall be no going in or out, or they shall be deserted by the inhabitants, that there shall be none to go in and out. Some understand it of the cities of Egypt, which was south from Judah; the places there whence they expected succours shall fail them, and they shall find no access to them. (2.) The inhabitants shall be hurried away into a foreign country, there to live in slavery: <hi type="italic">Judah shall be carried away captive.</hi> Some were already carried off, which they hoped might serve to answer the prediction, and that the residue should still be left; but no: <hi type="italic">It shall be carried away all of it.</hi> God will make a full end with them: <hi type="italic">It shall be wholly carried away.</hi> So it was in the last captivity under Zedekiah, because they repented not. (3.) navigation_sections.content_plain: Still the prophet is attempting to awaken this secure and stubborn people to repentance, by the consideration of the judgments of God that were coming upon them. He is to tell them, I. By the sign of a girdle spoiled that their pride should be stained, ver. 1-11 . II. By the sign of bottles filled with wine that their counsels should be blasted, ver. 12-14 . III. In consideration hereof he is to call them to repent and humble themselves, ver. 15-21 . IV. He is to convince them that it is for their obstinacy and incorrigibleness that the judgments of God are so prolonged and brought to extremity, ver. 22-27 .
